previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and peripheral vascular disease, was admitted with persistent diarrhea and abdominal cramping for 12 days. He was found to have a recurrent C. difficile infection, likely triggered by recent antibiotic use during a prior hospitalization. He also presented with acute kidney injury, attributed to dehydration and tacrolimus toxicity, with his level elevated to 11.5. IV fluids were administered, tacrolimus was reduced to 2 mg twice daily, and home diuretics were held. His renal function improved, with creatinine decreasing from 2.8 to 2.0. Atrial fibrillation with rapid rate was managed by transitioning to metoprolol for rate control, then back to carvedilol. His INR was initially elevated at 3.7, prompting temporary discontinuation of warfarin; it was restarted at 1.5 mg daily with a therapeutic INR of 3.2 at discharge. The patient completed initiation of a vancomycin taper for C. diff and was scheduled for a fecal transplant evaluation. He was discharged home with services, on adjusted immunosuppression, anticoagulation, and insulin therapy, with follow-up arranged with transplant, heart failure, and primary care teams.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to ___ after a fall after taking Tylenol ___. 
You sustained multiple right sided rib fractures and a small 
lung injury which is stable. You also fractured part of your 
lumbar spine vertebrae, but this fracture is non-operative and 
will heal with time, similarly to the rib fractures. 

Due to the contrast that you had received during evaluation of 
these fractures, you developed kidney failure, became very 
confused, and required dialysis. You became less confused after 
dialysis. Your renal function improved and you no longer needed 
dialysis. We also discovered that you had a urinary tract 
infection which we treated with antibiotics. 

WHAT TO DO FOR YOUR RIB FRACTURES:
* Your injury caused 5 rib fractures which can cause severe pain 
and subsequently cause you to take shallow breaths because of 
the pain.
* You should take your pain medication as directed to stay ahead 
of the pain otherwise you won't be able to take deep breaths. If 
the pain medication is too sedating take half the dose and 
notify your physician.
* Pneumonia is a complication of rib fractures.  In order to 
decrease your risk you must use your incentive spirometer 4 
times every hour while awake.  This will help expand the small 
airways in your lungs and assist in coughing up secretions that 
pool in the lungs.
* You will be more comfortable if you use a cough pillow to hold 
against your chest and guard your rib cage while coughing and 
deep breathing.
* Symptomatic relief with ice packs or heating pads for short 
periods may ease the pain.
* Return to the Emergency Room right away for any acute 
shortness of breath, increased pain or crackling sensation 
around your ribs (crepitus).

Please take care, we wish you the very ___!

Sincerely,
Your ___ Care Team

PROCEDURE:  PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks,
benefits and alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was
obtained from the healthcare proxy. The patient was then brought to the
angiography suite and placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure
time-out was performed per ___ protocol. The neck was prepped and draped in
the usual sterile fashion.
Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent right internal jugular vein
was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle. Permanent
ultrasound images were obtained before and after intravenous access, which
confirmed vein patency. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed into the right
atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and a short ___ wire was advanced into the IVC.
After sequential dilation of the soft tissue tract using 12 ___ and 14
___ dilators, a triple lumen 14 ___ hemodialysis catheter was advanced
over the wire into the superior vena cava with the tip in the distal SVC.  All
access ports were aspirated, flushed and capped. The catheter was secured to
the skin with a 0 silk suture and sterile dressings were applied. Final spot
fluoroscopic image demonstrating good alignment of the catheter and no
kinking.
The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complications.

Patent right internal jugular vein. Final fluoroscopic image showing triple
lumen temporary hemodialysis catheter with catheter tip terminating in the
distal superior vena cava.

Successful placement of a right internal jugular approach triple lumen
temporary hemodialysis catheter.  The line is read to use.
